theorem pilot_p002 {L₁ : Type u_1} {L₂ : Type u_2} {M : Type u_3} [Bracket L₁ L₂] [Bracket L₁ M]
  [Bracket L₂ M] [Bracket L₂ L₁] [AddCommGroup M] [IsLieTower L₁ L₂ M] [IsLieTower L₂ L₁ M] (x : L₁) (y : L₂) (m : M) :
  ⁅⁅x, y⁆, m⁆ = -⁅⁅y, x⁆, m⁆
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $L_1$, $L_2$ and $M$ be three types (sets). Assume given four binary operations, each written $\lbrack\cdot,\cdot\rbrack$: a map $L_1\times L_2\to L_2$, a map $L_1\times M\to M$, a map $L_2\times M\to M$, and a map $L_2\times L_1\to L_1$ (no axioms such as bilinearity are assumed for any of them). Assume $M$ is an abelian group (written additively), so that $M$ has addition and negation. Assume the two Leibniz-rule conditions hold: (i) for all $x\in L_1$, $y\in L_2$, $m\in M$, $\lbrack x,\lbrack y,m\rbrack\rbrack=\lbrack\lbrack x,y\rbrack,m\rbrack+\lbrack y,\lbrack x,m\rbrack\rbrack$ (this is the statement that $(L_1,L_2,M)$ is a "Lie tower"); and (ii) for all $y\in L_2$, $x\in L_1$, $m\in M$, $\lbrack y,\lbrack x,m\rbrack\rbrack=\lbrack\lbrack y,x\rbrack,m\rbrack+\lbrack x,\lbrack y,m\rbrack\rbrack$ (the same condition with the roles of $L_1$ and $L_2$ exchanged). Then for all $x\in L_1$, $y\in L_2$, $m\in M$ we have $\lbrack\lbrack x,y\rbrack,m\rbrack=-\lbrack\lbrack y,x\rbrack,m\rbrack$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $L_1, L_2, M$ be types with bracket operations $[\cdot,\cdot]$ on $L_1\times L_2$, on $L_1\times M$, on $L_2\times M$ and on $L_2\times L_1$, and suppose $M$ is an additive commutative group. Assume the Leibniz (Lie tower) identity holds for the triple $(L_1,L_2,M)$ and for the triple $(L_2,L_1,M)$, that is, $[x,[y,m]]=[[x,y],m]+[y,[x,m]]$ for $x\in L_1$, $y\in L_2$, $m\in M$, and $[y,[x,m]]=[[y,x],m]+[x,[y,m]]$. Then for all $x\in L_1$, $y\in L_2$, $m\in M$ we have $[[x,y],m]=-[[y,x],m]$.
proof_strategy: Write the two Leibniz identities for the pairs $(x,y)$ and $(y,x)$ and subtract them so that the doubly nested terms cancel.
faithful_informal_proof: Fix $x,y,m$ and put $A=\lbrack\lbrack x,y\rbrack,m\rbrack$, $B=\lbrack\lbrack y,x\rbrack,m\rbrack$, $P=\lbrack y,\lbrack x,m\rbrack\rbrack$, $Q=\lbrack x,\lbrack y,m\rbrack\rbrack$. Condition (i) gives $Q=A+P$ and condition (ii) gives $P=B+Q$. Hence $A+P=Q$ and, subtracting the second from the first (i.e. forming $(A+P)-P = Q-(B+Q)$ in the abelian group $M$), $A=-B$, which is the claim.
used_key_ideas: Leibniz rule for a tower of bracket actions, applied twice with the roles of x and y swapped
cancellation in an abelian group

theorem pilot_p003 (N : ℕ) :
  (Subgroup.map (Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.mapGL ℝ) (CongruenceSubgroup.Gamma1 N)).strictWidthInfty = 1
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $N$ be a natural number (the case $N=0$ is allowed, where congruence modulo $0$ means equality). Let $\Gamma_1(N)\subseteq \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ be the subgroup of integer matrices $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ of determinant $1$ with $a\equiv 1$ and $c\equiv 0 \pmod N$ (so that also $d\equiv 1 \pmod N$). Map $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ into $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb R)$ by viewing integer matrices as real matrices, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb R)$ be the image of $\Gamma_1(N)$ under this map. For a subgroup $\mathcal G$ of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb R)$, the set of strict periods is the additive subgroup of those $x\in\mathbb R$ with $\begin{pmatrix}1&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathcal G$, and the strict width of the cusp $\infty$ is the real number $x$ with (strict periods) $=\mathbb Z x$, or $0$ if there is no such $x$. The theorem states that the strict width of the cusp $\infty$ of $\mathcal G$ equals $1$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $N$ be a natural number and let $\Gamma_1(N)\subseteq SL_2(\mathbb Z)$ be the congruence subgroup of matrices congruent to $\begin{pmatrix}1&*\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ modulo $N$. Consider its image in $GL_2(\mathbb R)$ under the natural map. The strict width of the cusp $\infty$ for this subgroup equals $1$.
proof_strategy: Show that the translation matrix $T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ lies in the subgroup and apply a general criterion saying that the strict width is $1$ whenever $T$ belongs to the subgroup.
faithful_informal_proof: The matrix $T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $1$, upper-left entry $1$ and lower-left entry $0$, so it lies in $\Gamma_1(N)$ for every $N$ (the congruence conditions $1\equiv 1$ and $0\equiv 0 \pmod N$ hold trivially); its image in $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb R)$ is therefore in $\mathcal G$. A general lemma asserts that if $T$ belongs to a subgroup $\mathcal G$ of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb R)$ (in the setting of that lemma) then the strict width of $\infty$ is $1$. Applying it gives the claim.

the translation T = [[1,1],[0,1]] belongs to Gamma_1(N)
criterion: T in subgroup implies strict width at infinity equals 1

The exact hypotheses of the general criterion (strictWidthInfty_eq_one_of_T_mem) are not visible; it is applied here with no extra hypotheses beyond T lying in the subgroup, which is what the proof shows.

theorem pilot_p004 {α : Type u} {β : Type v} {γ : Type w} {δ : Type u_2} [PartialOrder α]
  [PartialOrder β] [Preorder γ] [Preorder δ] {f : α → γ} {g : β → δ} (hf : StrictAnti f) (hg : StrictAnti g) :
  StrictAnti (Prod.map f g)
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $(A,\le)$ and $(B,\le)$ be partially ordered sets and let $(C,\le)$ and $(D,\le)$ be preordered sets (the four sets live in arbitrary, possibly different, universes). A map $u\colon P\to Q$ between preordered sets is called strictly antitone if $x<y$ implies $u(y)<u(x)$, where $x<y$ means $x\le y$ and $y\not\le x$. Let $f\colon A\to C$ and $g\colon B\to D$ both be strictly antitone. Equip $A\times B$ and $C\times D$ with the product (componentwise) preorder, so $(a,b)\le(a',b')$ iff $a\le a'$ and $b\le b'$, with the induced strict order. Then the product map $f\times g\colon A\times B\to C\times D$, $(a,b)\mapsto (f(a),g(b))$, is strictly antitone.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be partially ordered sets and $\gamma,\delta$ preordered sets. Let $f:\alpha\to\gamma$ and $g:\beta\to\delta$ be strictly antitone (that is, $a<b$ implies $f(b)<f(a)$, and likewise for $g$). Then the product map $(a,b)\mapsto(f(a),g(b))$ from $\alpha\times\beta$ to $\gamma\times\delta$ is strictly antitone for the product orders.
proof_strategy: Characterise strict inequality in a product as "strict in one coordinate and non-strict in the other", then use that a strictly antitone map is in particular antitone.
faithful_informal_proof: Take $(a_1,a_2)<(b_1,b_2)$ in $A\times B$. Since $A,B$ are partial orders, this holds iff ($a_1<b_1$ and $a_2\le b_2$) or ($a_1\le b_1$ and $a_2<b_2$). Case 1: $a_1<b_1$ gives $f(b_1)<f(a_1)$ because $f$ is strictly antitone, and $a_2\le b_2$ gives $g(b_2)\le g(a_2)$ because $g$, being strictly antitone, is antitone. Case 2: symmetric, $f(b_1)\le f(a_1)$ from antitonicity of $f$ and $g(b_2)<g(a_2)$ from strict antitonicity of $g$. In either case ($f(b_1)<f(a_1)$ and $g(b_2)\le g(a_2)$) or ($f(b_1)\le f(a_1)$ and $g(b_2)<g(a_2)$) holds, which is exactly $(f(b_1),g(b_2))<(f(a_1),g(a_2))$ in $C\times D$. Hence $f\times g$ is strictly antitone.
used_key_ideas: Strict order on a product: strict in one coordinate and weak in the other
Strictly antitone implies antitone (needs the domain to be a partial order)
Case split on which coordinate is strict

u$ is the finite sum $\int f\,d

Let $\iota$ be a countable index type (possibly empty) and let $(s_i)_{i\in\iota}$ be a family of arbitrary subsets of $\alpha$ (no measurability is assumed) which is directed under inclusion: for all $i,j\in\iota$ there is $k\in\iota$ with $s_i\subseteq s_k$ and $s_j\subseteq s_k$. For a set $s$, $\mu|_s$ denotes the restriction of $\mu$ to $s$, the measure $A\mapsto \mu(A\cap s)$. Then

theorem_in_words_v1: Let $(\alpha,\mathcal M)$ be a measurable space, $\mu$ a measure on it, $f:\alpha\to[0,\infty]$ a simple function (measurable with finitely many values), and $(s_i)_{i\in\iota}$ a countable family of subsets of $\alpha$ that is directed under inclusion (any two members are contained in a third). Then the integral of $f$ with respect to the restriction of $\mu$ to $\bigcup_i s_i$ equals the supremum over $i$ of the integral of $f$ with respect to the restriction of $\mu$ to $s_i$.
proof_strategy: Expand the simple-function integral as a finite sum over values, use continuity of the restricted measure along a directed countable union on the measurable level sets, pull the supremum out of the products, and then interchange the finite sum with the directed supremum.
faithful_informal_proof:
Unfold the integral of the simple function $f$ as $\sum_{r\in f(\alpha)} r\,
u(f^{-1}\{r\})$ for $
u=\mu|_{ igcup_i s_i}$ and for $
u=\mu|_{s_i}$. Each level set $f^{-1}\{r\}$ is measurable, so for a directed countable family of sets the restricted measure of the union satisfies $\mu|_{ igcup_i s_i}(f^{-1}\{r\})=\sup_i \mu|_{s_i}(f^{-1}\{r\})$. In $[0,\infty]$ multiplication by $r$ commutes with suprema, $r\cdot\sup_i a_i=\sup_i r a_i$. The left side thus becomes $\sum_{r}\sup_i r\,\mu|_{s_i}(f^{-1}\{r\})$, and we must show this equals $\sup_i\sum_r r\,\mu|_{s_i}(f^{-1}\{r\})$. This is the interchange of a finite sum with a supremum over a directed family: it holds as soon as the family of summand-functions $i\mapsto (r\mapsto r\,\mu|_{s_i}(f^{-1}\{r\}))$ is directed in the pointwise order. Given $i,j$, directedness of $(s_i)$ gives $k$ with $s_i,s_j\subseteq s_k$, and then for every $r$ both $r\,\mu|_{s_i}(f^{-1}\{r\})$ and $r\,\mu|_{s_j}(f^{-1}\{r\})$ are $\le r\,\mu|_{s_k}(f^{-1}\{r\})$ by monotonicity of the measure in the restricting set and monotonicity of multiplication.

theorem pilot_p006 {V : Type u_1} {P : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup V]
  [InnerProductSpace ℝ V] [MetricSpace P] [NormedAddTorsor V P] [hd2 : Fact (Module.finrank ℝ V = 2)]
  [Module.Oriented ℝ V (Fin 2)] (t : Affine.Triangle ℝ P) {i₁ i₂ i₃ : Fin 3} (h₁₂ : i₁ ≠ i₂) (h₁₃ : i₁ ≠ i₃)
  (h₂₃ : i₂ ≠ i₃) (signs : Finset (Fin 3)) :
  2 • EuclideanGeometry.oangle (t.points i₂) (t.points i₁) (Affine.Simplex.excenter t signs) =
    2 • EuclideanGeometry.oangle (Affine.Simplex.excenter t signs) (t.points i₁) (t.points i₃)
theorem_in_words_v2:
Let $V$ be a real inner product space of dimension exactly $2$, equipped with an orientation, and let $P$ be a Euclidean affine space modelled on $V$ (a metric space with a normed torsor structure over $V$). Let $t$ be a (nondegenerate) triangle in $P$, i.e. an affinely independent triple of points $t_0,t_1,t_2$ of $P$. Let $i_1,i_2,i_3\in\{0,1,2\}$ be pairwise distinct indices, and let $\mathrm{signs}\subseteq\{0,1,2\}$ be an arbitrary subset; let $E$ be the excenter of $t$ attached to $\mathrm{signs}$ (the centre of the corresponding sphere tangent to the three side lines of the triangle; the choice $\mathrm{signs}=\emptyset$ gives the incenter). Write $\angle(A,B,C)\in\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ for the oriented angle at the vertex $B$ from the ray $BA$ to the ray $BC$. Then
$$2\cdot\angle(t_{i_2},t_{i_1},E)\;=\;2\cdot\angle(E,t_{i_1},t_{i_3})\quad\text{in }\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z},$$
that is, the two oriented angles are equal modulo $\pi$: the excenter lies on a bisector (internal or external) of the angle of the triangle at the vertex $t_{i_1}$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $V$ be a $2$-dimensional oriented real inner product space and $P$ a Euclidean affine space over $V$ (a metric space with a normed torsor structure). Let $t$ be a triangle in $P$, let $i_1,i_2,i_3$ be three pairwise distinct indices in $\{0,1,2\}$ and let $E$ be the excenter of $t$ corresponding to a chosen subset of signs $\mathrm{signs}\subseteq\{0,1,2\}$ (this family includes the incenter). Write $A_k$ for the vertex of index $k$. Then, for oriented angles modulo $2\pi$, $2\angle(A_{i_2},A_{i_1},E)=2\angle(E,A_{i_1},A_{i_3})$. Equivalently, $E$ lies on a bisector of the angle at $A_{i_1}$ modulo $\pi$.
proof_strategy: Translate the angle equality into equality of distances from the excenter to the two side lines through $t_{i_1}$, and use that an excenter is equidistant from all three side lines.
faithful_informal_proof: By the preceding criterion, for a point $p$ the distance from $p$ to the line through $t_{i_1},t_{i_2}$ (the face opposite $t_{i_3}$) equals the distance from $p$ to the line through $t_{i_1},t_{i_3}$ (the face opposite $t_{i_2}$) if and only if $2\angle(t_{i_2},t_{i_1},p)=2\angle(p,t_{i_1},t_{i_3})$. Rewriting the goal backwards with this criterion (for $p=E$) turns it into equality of the distances from $E$ to these two side lines. Each such distance is the distance from $E$ to its orthogonal projection onto the side line, i.e. to the corresponding touchpoint of the exsphere. Since $E$ is the centre of an exsphere, its distances to the touchpoints on the faces are all equal to the exsphere radius, and the equality follows.
used_key_ideas: An oriented angle equation modulo $\pi$ (doubling the angle) is equivalent to equidistance from the two side lines through the vertex
The excenter is equidistant from the three side lines (touchpoints of the exsphere)
Distance to a line equals distance to the orthogonal projection onto it
possible_uncertainties_v2: The definition of the excenter and of signs (which subset gives the incenter) is not in the file context; the description of the excenter as the centre of a sphere tangent to the side lines, and signs = empty giving the incenter, is from general knowledge.
The Lean statement writes the factor 2 as a natural-number scalar and the source as an integer scalar; these agree in the group of angles.

theorem pilot_p007 {R : Type u_1} [Ring R] {M : Type u_2} [AddCommGroup M]
  [_root_.Module R M] {N : Type u_3} [AddCommGroup N] [_root_.Module R N] {f : M →ₗ[R] N} : f.range.FG ↔ f.ker.CoFG
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $R$ be a (not necessarily commutative) ring with identity, let $M$ and $N$ be left $R$-modules (in particular additive abelian groups), and let $f\colon M\to N$ be an $R$-linear map. Call a submodule $S$ of a module $M$ \emph{co-finitely generated} if the quotient module $M/S$ is a finitely generated $R$-module. Then the range (image) $f(M)$ is a finitely generated submodule of $N$ if and only if the kernel $\ker f$ is a co-finitely generated submodule of $M$, i.e. if and only if $M/\ker f$ is a finitely generated $R$-module.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $R$ be a ring, $M$ and $N$ be left $R$-modules and $f:M\to N$ an $R$-linear map. Then the range of $f$ is a finitely generated submodule of $N$ if and only if the kernel of $f$ is cofinitely generated, meaning that the quotient $M/\ker f$ is a finitely generated module.
proof_strategy: Rewrite finite generation of the submodule $\operatorname{range} f$ as finite generation of $\operatorname{range} f$ regarded as a module, and use the first isomorphism theorem $M/\ker f\cong \operatorname{range} f$.
faithful_informal_proof: A submodule is finitely generated exactly when it is finitely generated as a module in its own right, so the claim becomes: $\operatorname{range} f$ is a finitely generated module iff $M/\ker f$ is. The first isomorphism theorem gives an $R$-linear isomorphism $M/\ker f\cong \operatorname{range} f$. Finite generation of a module is invariant under linear isomorphism (images of generating sets under an isomorphism, and of its inverse, are generating sets), so $M/\ker f$ is finitely generated iff $\operatorname{range} f$ is.
used_key_ideas: first isomorphism theorem $M/\ker f\cong \operatorname{range} f$
finite generation of a submodule equals finite generation of it as a module
finite generation is invariant under linear isomorphism

theorem pilot_p008 {R : Type u_1} {A : Type u_2} {p : A → Prop} [CommSemiring R] [StarRing R] [MetricSpace R]
  [IsTopologicalSemiring R] [ContinuousStar R] [TopologicalSpace A] [Ring A] [StarRing A] [Algebra R A]
  [instCFC : ContinuousFunctionalCalculus R A p] (f g : R → R) (a : A) : Commute (cfc f a) (cfc g a)
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring equipped with a star operation (so $R$ is a star ring), a metric space structure, such that $R$ is a topological semiring (addition and multiplication are continuous) and the star operation $R\to R$ is continuous. Let $A$ be a (not necessarily commutative) ring with a star operation (a star ring) and with some topology (no compatibility of this topology with the ring structure is assumed), and suppose $A$ is an $R$-algebra. Let $p$ be a predicate on $A$ such that $A$ carries a continuous functional calculus over $R$ for the elements satisfying $p$. By definition this means: for every $a\in A$ with $p(a)$ there is a star algebra homomorphism $\Phi_a\colon C(\sigma_R(a),R)\to A$ (here $\sigma_R(a)=\{r\in R : r\cdot 1-a \text{ is not a unit of } A\}$ is the spectrum of $a$, topologised as a subspace of $R$, and $C(\cdot,R)$ is the star $R$-algebra of continuous $R$-valued functions under pointwise operations) which sends the restriction of the identity function to $a$, is continuous and injective, has the spectrum of $\Phi_a(f)$ equal to the range of $f$, and preserves $p$; moreover $p(0)$ holds and the spectrum $\sigma_R(a)$ is compact. For arbitrary functions $f\colon R\to R$ and $a\in A$ one then writes $f(a)$ (the functional calculus) for $\Phi_a(f|_{\sigma_R(a)})$ if $p(a)$ holds and $f$ is continuous on $\sigma_R(a)$, and $f(a):=0$ otherwise. The statement: for all (arbitrary, not necessarily continuous) functions $f,g\colon R\to R$ and every $a\in A$, the elements $f(a)$ and $g(a)$ commute, i.e. $f(a)\,g(a)=g(a)\,f(a)$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring with a star operation and a metric, which is a topological semiring with continuous star. Let $A$ be a topological ring with star operation that is an $R$-algebra, and let $p$ be a predicate on $A$ such that $A$ has a continuous functional calculus for $R$ relative to $p$. Then for any two functions $f,g:R\to R$ and any $a\in A$, the elements $f(a)$ and $g(a)$ defined by the functional calculus commute, i.e. $f(a)g(a)=g(a)f(a)$. (By convention $f(a)=0$ when the functional calculus does not apply.)
proof_strategy: Split according to whether each of $f(a)$, $g(a)$ is the junk value $0$ or an honest image under $\Phi_a$; zero commutes with everything, and two images under a ring homomorphism of elements of the commutative ring $C(\sigma_R(a),R)$ commute.
faithful_informal_proof: We use the case-distinction principle for the functional calculus: to prove a property $P$ of $f(a)$ it suffices to prove $P(0)$ and to prove $P(\Phi_a(\tilde f))$ whenever $p(a)$ holds and $f$ is continuous on $\sigma_R(a)$, where $\tilde f$ is the restriction of $f$ to the spectrum as a continuous function. Apply this to $P(x):=$ "$x$ commutes with $g(a)$" and the element $f(a)$. The case $P(0)$ holds since $0$ commutes with everything. In the remaining case $f(a)=\Phi_a(\tilde f)$ and we must show $\Phi_a(\tilde f)$ commutes with $g(a)$. Apply the principle again, now to $P'(x):=$ "$\Phi_a(\tilde f)$ commutes with $x$" and the element $g(a)$. Again $P'(0)$ is trivial, and in the remaining case $g(a)=\Phi_a(\tilde g)$ for a continuous $\tilde g$. Now $\tilde f$ and $\tilde g$ lie in $C(\sigma_R(a),R)$, which is a commutative ring because $R$ is a commutative semiring and operations are pointwise, so $\tilde f\tilde g=\tilde g\tilde f$. A ring homomorphism preserves commuting pairs, so $\Phi_a(\tilde f)\Phi_a(\tilde g)=\Phi_a(\tilde f\tilde g)=\Phi_a(\tilde g\tilde f)=\Phi_a(\tilde g)\Phi_a(\tilde f)$.
used_key_ideas: junk-value convention: f(a)=0 when p(a) fails or f is not continuous on the spectrum
case split via a lemma reducing a property of f(a) to the degenerate case and the case of an image under the functional calculus homomorphism
C(spectrum, R) is commutative since R is a commutative semiring
ring (algebra) homomorphisms preserve commuting elements

Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb R$ (with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra), let $E$ be a real normed vector space (a normed additive commutative group with a normed space structure over $\mathbb R$; completeness is not assumed), and let $f\colon\mathbb R\to E$ be an arbitrary function (no measurability or integrability assumed). Let $\iota$ be a type, $l$ a filter on $\iota$ that is countably generated (it need not be non-trivial), and $b\colon\iota\to\mathbb R$ a function with $b(i)\to+\infty$ along $l$. The integral $\int_{(b(i),\infty)} f\,d\mu$ is the Bochner integral over the open half-line, with the usual convention that it equals $0$ when $f$ is not integrable on that half-line. Then
$$\int_{(b(i),\infty)} f\,d\mu\;\longrightarrow\;0\quad\text{as } i\to l,$$
i.e. the function $i\mapsto\int_{(b(i),\infty)}f\,d\mu$ tends to $0\in E$ along $l$.

Then $\int_{(b(i),\infty)}f\,d\mu$ tends to $0$ along $l$. (No integrability of $f$ is assumed; the integral of a non-integrable function is taken to be $0$.)

faithful_informal_proof: Case 1: $f$ is not integrable on $(a,\infty)$ for any $a$. Then for every $i$ the integral over $(b(i),\infty)$ is $0$ by the convention for non-integrable functions, so the function is identically $0$ and tends to $0$. Case 2: there is $a$ with $f$ integrable on $(a,\infty)$. Since $b\to+\infty$ along $l$, eventually along $l$ we have $b(i)\ge a$; for such $i$, $(b(i),\infty)\subseteq(a,\infty)$, so $f$ is integrable on $(b(i),\infty)$ and additivity of the integral over $(a,b(i)]\sqcup(b(i),\infty)=(a,\infty)$ gives $\int_{(a,\infty)}f\,d\mu-\int_a^{b(i)}f\,d\mu=\int_{(b(i),\infty)}f\,d\mu$. By the convergence theorem for interval integrals (the sets $(-\infty,b(i)]$ form an a.e.-cover of $(a,\infty)$ w.r.t. $\mu$ restricted to $(a,\infty)$ along the countably generated filter, and $f$ is integrable there), $\int_a^{b(i)}f\,d\mu\to\int_{(a,\infty)}f\,d\mu$ along $l$. Hence the left side tends to $\int_{(a,\infty)}f\,d\mu-\int_{(a,\infty)}f\,d\mu=0$, and since the tail integral agrees with it eventually along $l$, it also tends to $0$.

Let $\alpha$ and $\Omega$ be measurable spaces, let $\kappa$ be a kernel from $\alpha$ to $\Omega$, let $\mu$ be a measure on $\alpha$, let $\iota,\iota'$ be index types, let $\pi\colon\iota\to\mathcal P(\mathcal P(\Omega))$ be a family of collections of subsets of $\Omega$ (no measurability or $\pi$-system assumption is made), and let $g\colon\iota'\to\iota$ be a bijection. $$\kappa(a)\Big(\bigcap_{i\in s}f_i\Big)=\prod_{i\in s}\kappa(a)(f_i).$$
Then the reindexed family $\pi\circ g=(\pi_{g(j)})_{j\in\iota'}$ is independent with respect to $\kappa$ and $\mu$ if and only if $\pi$ is independent with respect to $\kappa$ and $\mu$.

Then the reindexed family $\pi\circ g$ is independent with respect to $\kappa$ and $\mu$ (independence of families of sets) if and only if $\pi$ is.

($\Leftarrow$, reindexing along the injective $g$.) Assume $\pi$ independent. Let $s\subseteq\iota'$ be finite and $f_j\in\pi_{g(j)}$ for $j\in s$. Define $f'\colon\iota\to\mathcal P(\Omega)$ by $f'(g(j))=f_j$ and $f'(i)=\emptyset$ for $i$ outside the image of $g$ (well defined since $g$ is injective). Then $f'_i\in\pi_i$ for all $i$ in the finite set $g(s)$. Applying independence of $\pi$ to the index set $g(s)$ and the sets $f'$ yields, for $\mu$-a.e. $a$, $\kappa(a)(\bigcap_{i\in g(s)}f'_i)=\prod_{i\in g(s)}\kappa(a)(f'_i)$. Since $g$ is injective, $\bigcap_{i\in g(s)}f'_i=\bigcap_{j\in s}f_j$ and $\prod_{i\in g(s)}\kappa(a)(f'_i)=\prod_{j\in s}\kappa(a)(f_j)$, which is the required identity for $\pi\circ g$.
($\Rightarrow$, along the surjective $g$.) Assume $\pi\circ g$ independent. As $g$ is surjective it has a right inverse $g'$ with $g\circ g'=\mathrm{id}$, and $g'$ is injective. By the previous direction applied to the family $\pi\circ g$ and $g'$, the family $(\pi\circ g)\circ g'=\pi\circ(g\circ g')=\pi$ is independent. The theorem follows for the bijection $g$ by combining the two directions.

  [MeasurableMul₂ M] {m : MeasurableSpace α} (s : Multiset (α → M)) (hs : ∀ f ∈ s, Measurable f) :

theorem_in_words_v2: Let $M$ be a commutative monoid carrying a measurable space structure such that multiplication $M\times M\to M$ is measurable with respect to the product $\sigma$-algebra on $M\times M$. Let $\alpha$ be a measurable space. Let $s$ be a finite multiset (repetitions counted) of functions $\alpha\to M$ such that every $f\in s$ is measurable. Then the function $\alpha\to M$, $x\mapsto \prod_{f\in s} f(x)$ (the product, with multiplicities, of the multiset $\{f(x): f\in s\}$ obtained by evaluating every member of $s$ at $x$) is measurable.

The value of this product at a point $x$ equals the product of the multiset $\{f(x):f\in s\}$ (evaluation at $x$ is a monoid homomorphism and commutes with multiset products). Rewriting the function $x\mapsto\prod_{f\in s}f(x)$ in this form gives exactly the product function, which is therefore measurable.

theorem_in_words_v2: Let $\mathrm{Cat}$ denote the category whose objects are small categories (at fixed universe levels: objects in one universe and morphism sets in another) and whose morphisms are functors. Then $\mathrm{Cat}$ has a terminal object, i.e. there is a category $T$ such that for every category $X$ there is exactly one functor $X\to T$ (the statement holds at all universe levels of $\mathrm{Cat}$).
theorem_in_words_v1: The category $\mathrm{Cat}$ of (small) categories has a terminal object.
proof_strategy: Exhibit the terminal object as the discrete category on a single point (with hom-sets lifted to the required universe), using the fact that a discrete category with a unique object is terminal in $\mathrm{Cat}$.
faithful_informal_proof: Take $T$ to be the category with one object $\ast$ and only the identity morphism, its morphism sets being transported into the appropriate universe by the hom-shrinking construction; one checks that it is discrete, i.e. its hom-types are subsingletons and any morphism between equal objects is the identity. A discrete category with a unique object is terminal in $\mathrm{Cat}$: for any category $X$, the constant functor with value $\ast$ is a functor $X\to T$, and any two functors $X\to T$ are equal because $T$ has only one object and at most one morphism between any two objects, so the functors agree on objects and on morphisms. Hence $T$ is terminal and $\mathrm{Cat}$ has a terminal object.

theorem pilot_p041 {R : Type u} [CommSemiring R] {r : R} (hr : IsUnit r) (s : Set R) :
  PrimeSpectrum.zeroLocus (r • s) = PrimeSpectrum.zeroLocus s
theorem_in_words_v2:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring and let $\operatorname{Spec}R$ denote its prime spectrum, i.e. the set of prime ideals of $R$. For a subset $s\subseteq R$ its zero locus is $V(s)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R : s\subseteq\mathfrak p\}$, the set of prime ideals containing $s$. Let $r\in R$ be a unit and $s\subseteq R$ an arbitrary subset, and let $r\cdot s=\{rx : x\in s\}$ be the pointwise multiple. Then
$$V(r\cdot s)=V(s).$$
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, $r\in R$ a unit, and $s\subseteq R$ any subset. Let $r\cdot s=\{rx : x\in s\}$. Then the zero locus of $r\cdot s$ in the prime spectrum of $R$ equals the zero locus of $s$, where the zero locus of a subset $t$ is the set of prime ideals $P$ with $t\subseteq P$.
proof_strategy: For a prime ideal $\mathfrak p$, show $r\cdot s\subseteq\mathfrak p\iff s\subseteq\mathfrak p$, because multiplying by a unit does not change membership in an ideal.
faithful_informal_proof: Fix a prime ideal $\mathfrak p$. Unfolding, $\mathfrak p\in V(r\cdot s)$ means that $y\in\mathfrak p$ for every $y\in r\cdot s$, i.e. $rx\in\mathfrak p$ for every $x\in s$ (using that $r\cdot s$ is the image of $s$ under multiplication by $r$). Since $r$ is a unit and $\mathfrak p$ is an ideal, $rx\in\mathfrak p\iff x\in\mathfrak p$ (if $x\in\mathfrak p$ then $rx\in\mathfrak p$; if $rx\in\mathfrak p$ then $x=r^{-1}(rx)\in\mathfrak p$). Hence the condition is equivalent to $x\in\mathfrak p$ for all $x\in s$, i.e. $\mathfrak p\in V(s)$.
used_key_ideas: multiplication by a unit preserves membership in an ideal
pointwise scalar multiple of a set is its image under multiplication
zero locus is the set of primes containing the set

theorem pilot_p042 {V : Type u} {G : SimpleGraph V} {u v : V} (p : G.Walk u v) (n : ℕ) :
  (p.drop n).length = p.length - n
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$, let $u,v\in V$, and let $p$ be a walk in $G$ from $u$ to $v$ (a sequence of vertices $u=v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k=v$ with $v_{i}\sim v_{i+1}$; its length $k$ is the number of edges). For a natural number $n$, let $p.\mathrm{drop}(n)$ be the walk obtained by removing the first $n$ edges of $p$: it starts at the $n$-th vertex $v_n$ of $p$ (taken to be $v$ when $n\ge k$) and ends at $v$, and it is the empty walk at $v$ if $n\ge k$. Then $$\operatorname{length}(p.\mathrm{drop}(n))=\operatorname{length}(p)-n,$$ where the subtraction is truncated subtraction on natural numbers (equal to $0$ if $n\ge\operatorname{length}(p)$).
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $G$ be a simple graph with vertex set $V$ and let $p$ be a walk in $G$ from $u$ to $v$. For a natural number $n$, let $p.\mathrm{drop}(n)$ be the walk obtained from $p$ by deleting its first $n$ edges, which is a walk from the $n$-th vertex of $p$ to $v$. Then the length of $p.\mathrm{drop}(n)$ equals $\mathrm{length}(p)-n$, where the subtraction is truncated at $0$ on natural numbers.
proof_strategy: Induct on the walk $p$ (generalizing over $n$), split on whether $n$ is $0$ or a successor, and simplify using the recursive definition of dropping.
faithful_informal_proof: Induct on $p$, for all $n$ simultaneously. If $p$ is the trivial walk, then dropping gives the trivial walk, of length $0=0-n$. If $p$ is an edge followed by a walk $q$, so $\operatorname{length}(p)=\operatorname{length}(q)+1$, split on $n$. For $n=0$ the drop is $p$ itself (up to re-labelling its start vertex), so its length is $\operatorname{length}(p)=\operatorname{length}(p)-0$. For $n+1$, the drop of $p$ is the drop of $q$ by $n$; by the induction hypothesis its length is $\operatorname{length}(q)-n=(\operatorname{length}(q)+1)-(n+1)$.
used_key_ideas: Structural induction on walks
Recursive definition of drop: trivial walk, $n=0$, and cons with successor
Truncated subtraction identity $(m+1)-(n+1)=m-n$

theorem pilot_p043 {β : Type u_2} [SemilatticeSup β] {D : Set (Set (β × β))} :
  ScottContinuousOn D fun x =>
    match x with
    | (a, b) => a ⊔ b
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $\beta$ be a join-semilattice (a set with a binary join $\sqcup$, giving the partial order $a\le b\iff a\sqcup b=b$). Equip $\beta\times\beta$ with the componentwise (product) order. Let $D$ be an arbitrary family of subsets of $\beta\times\beta$. Then the join map $\beta\times\beta\to\beta$, $(a,b)\mapsto a\sqcup b$, is Scott continuous on $D$. Here a map $f:\alpha\to\beta'$ between preordered sets is Scott continuous on a family $D$ of subsets of $\alpha$ if, for every $d\in D$ that is nonempty and directed (every two elements of $d$ have an upper bound in $d$) and every $a$ that is a least upper bound of $d$, the element $f(a)$ is a least upper bound of the image $f(d)$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $\beta$ be a join-semilattice (a set with a binary supremum $\sqcup$), give $\beta\times\beta$ the product order, and let $D$ be any family of subsets of $\beta\times\beta$. Then the map $(a,b)\mapsto a\sqcup b$ from $\beta\times\beta$ to $\beta$ is Scott continuous on $D$. That is, for every $d\in D$ that is nonempty and directed, and every least upper bound $a$ of $d$, the image of $d$ under the map has least upper bound equal to the value of the map at $a$.
proof_strategy: The statement follows from full Scott continuity of the join, which is proved directly: the join preserves directed suprema in the product order.
faithful_informal_proof: Scott continuity on any family $D$ follows from Scott continuity on all nonempty directed sets, so it suffices to treat that case. Let $d\subseteq\beta\times\beta$ be nonempty and directed with least upper bound $(p_1,p_2)$. We show $p_1\sqcup p_2$ is the least upper bound of $\{b_1\sqcup b_2\mid (b_1,b_2)\in d\}$. Upper bound: for $(b_1,b_2)\in d$ we have $b_1\le p_1$ and $b_2\le p_2$, hence $b_1\sqcup b_2\le p_1\sqcup p_2$ by monotonicity of the join. Least: let $b$ be an upper bound of the image, i.e. $b_1\sqcup b_2\le b$ for all $(b_1,b_2)\in d$. Then $b_1\le b$ and $b_2\le b$, so $(b,b)$ is an upper bound of $d$, hence $(p_1,p_2)\le(b,b)$ since $(p_1,p_2)$ is the least upper bound. Thus $p_1\le b$ and $p_2\le b$, so $p_1\sqcup p_2\le b$.

join is monotone
componentwise order on products

Assume that $c$ is a limit cone, and that every projection $c_i$ is an epimorphism in $\mathrm{Profinite}$ (i.e. a surjective continuous map). Let $\mathcal D$ be the category of structured arrows from $c.\mathrm{pt}$ along $\iota$: its objects are pairs $(X,f)$ with $X$ a finite set and $f:c.\mathrm{pt}\to\iota X$ a continuous map, and a morphism $(X,f)\to(X',f')$ is a map $s:X\to X'$ of finite sets with $\iota(s)\circ f=f'$. Let $E:I\to\mathcal D$ be the functor sending $i$ to $(F(i),c_i)$ and a morphism $\varphi:i\to j$ to $F(\varphi)$. Then $E$ is an initial functor: for every object $d$ of $\mathcal D$ the comma category of objects $i\in I$ together with a morphism $E(i)\to d$ is nonempty and connected.

Let $c$ be a cone over the composite of $F$ with the inclusion of finite sets into profinite sets, and suppose $c$ is a limit cone and every projection $c_i: c.\mathrm{pt}\to F(i)$ is an epimorphism. Consider the functor from $I$ to the comma category whose objects are pairs $(X,f)$ with $X$ a finite set and $f:c.\mathrm{pt}\to X$ a morphism of profinite sets, which sends $i$ to $(F(i),c_i)$ and sends a morphism $\varphi$ to $F(\varphi)$. Then this functor is initial.

First, replace $I$ by the equivalent category $\mathrm{ULiftHom}(\mathrm{ULift}\, I)$ (an equivalence $e$ with inverse $e^{-1}$); since initiality is invariant under precomposition with an equivalence, it suffices to prove that $e^{-1}\circ E$ is initial. For a functor out of a cofiltered category, being initial is equivalent to two conditions on each target object $d=(X,f)$: (1) there exist $i\in I$ and a morphism $E(i)\to d$; (2) for any $i$ and any two morphisms $s,s':E(i)\to d$ there exist $j$ and $u:j\to i$ with $E(u)$ composed with $s$ equal to $E(u)$ composed with $s'$.

This gives the required morphism $E(i)\to d$.

theorem pilot_p045 (a : Ordinal) {b : Ordinal} (hb₁ : b ≠ 1)
  (hb : Ordinal.IsPrincipal (fun x1 x2 => x1 + x2) b) : Ordinal.IsPrincipal (fun x1 x2 => x1 + x2) (a * b)
theorem_in_words_v2: Work with ordinals (in a fixed universe). Say an ordinal $o$ is additively principal if for all ordinals $x,y<o$ one has $x+y<o$ (that is, the set of ordinals below $o$ is closed under ordinal addition; by convention $0$ counts as additively principal). Let $a$ be any ordinal and let $b$ be an ordinal with $b\neq 1$ which is additively principal. Then the ordinal product $a\cdot b$ is additively principal.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $a$ and $b$ be ordinals with $b\ne 1$, and suppose $b$ is additively principal, meaning that $x+y<b$ whenever $x,y<b$. Then $a\cdot b$ is additively principal.
proof_strategy: Dispose of the cases $a=0$ and $b=0$, where the product is $0$. Otherwise $b>1$ is additively principal, hence a limit ordinal, so elements below $a b$ lie below some $a x$ with $x<b$, and sums can be bounded using $a x+a y=a(x+y)$ with $x+y<b$.
faithful_informal_proof: If $a=0$, then $a\cdot b=0$, and $0$ is additively principal (there are no ordinals below it). If $b=0$, then $a\cdot b=0$ again. So assume $b>0$, i.e. $1\le b$; together with $b\ne1$ this gives $1<b$. An additively principal ordinal larger than $1$ is a limit ordinal (it has no immediate predecessor), so $b$ is a limit ordinal. For a limit ordinal $b$ we have $c<a\cdot b$ iff there is $x<b$ with $c<a\cdot x$. Now let $c,d<a\cdot b$. Choose $x<b$ with $c<a x$ and $y<b$ with $d<a y$. Since $b$ is additively principal, $x+y<b$. By left distributivity $a(x+y)=ax+ay$, and $c+d<ax+ay$ because ordinal addition is strictly increasing in the right argument and weakly increasing in the left argument ($c+d< c+ay\le ax+ay$). Thus $c+d<a(x+y)$ with $x+y<b$, which by the same characterisation of elements below $a\cdot b$ shows $c+d<a\cdot b$.

For limit $b$: $c<ab\iff\exists x<b,\ c<ax$
Left distributivity $a(x+y)=ax+ay$

$$\partial(\mathcal A^{c})=(\partial^{+}\mathcal A)^{c},$$
i.e. the shadow of the family of complements equals the family of complements of the upper shadow.

Then the (lower) shadow of $\mathcal A^{c}$, the family of sets obtained by removing one element from a member, equals the family of complements of the members of the upper shadow of $\mathcal A$, where the upper shadow of $\mathcal A$ is the family of sets obtained by adding one element not already present to a member.

Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent under $P$ (weak Markov property): the $\sigma$-algebras they generate on $\Omega$ are $P$-independent, i.e. $P(X\in A,\,Y\in A')=P(X\in A)\,P(Y\in A')$ for measurable $A,A'$ in the product $\sigma$-algebras.

  {φ : L.BoundedFormula α (n + 1)} : FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.sigmaAll ⟨n + 1, φ⟩ = ⟨n, φ.all⟩
theorem_in_words_v2:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, $\alpha$ a type (of free variable names) and $n\in\mathbb N$. A bounded formula $\varphi\in L.\mathrm{BoundedFormula}(\alpha,n)$ is a first-order $L$-formula whose free variables are indexed by $\alpha$ together with $n$ additional (de Bruijn-style) variables indexed by $\mathrm{Fin}\,n$; if $\varphi\in L.\mathrm{BoundedFormula}(\alpha,n+1)$ then $\forall\varphi\in L.\mathrm{BoundedFormula}(\alpha,n)$ denotes the universal quantification of $\varphi$ over its last bound variable. Let $\mathrm{sigmaAll}$ be the function on dependent pairs $(k,\psi)$ with $k\in\mathbb N$ and $\psi\in L.\mathrm{BoundedFormula}(\alpha,k)$, defined by $\mathrm{sigmaAll}(k+1,\psi)=(k,\forall\psi)$ and, for $k=0$, by returning the default element. The statement: for every $\varphi\in L.\mathrm{BoundedFormula}(\alpha,n+1)$,
$$\mathrm{sigmaAll}\,(n+1,\varphi)=(n,\forall\varphi)$$
as an equality of dependent pairs.
theorem_in_words_v1: Consider first-order formulas over a language $L$ with free variables indexed by $\alpha$, where the formula is allowed $n$ extra bound variables, packaged as pairs $(n,\varphi)$ with $\varphi$ a bounded formula with $n$ bound variables. There is a function `sigmaAll` on such pairs that quantifies universally over the last bound variable when there is one. The statement is: for $\varphi$ a bounded formula with $n+1$ bound variables, $\mathrm{sigmaAll}(n+1,\varphi)=(n,\forall\varphi)$, where $\forall\varphi$ is the universal quantification of $\varphi$ over its last bound variable.
proof_strategy: This is the successor clause of the definition of the function.
faithful_informal_proof: By the defining clause of sigmaAll on pairs with positive first component, $(n+1,\varphi)\mapsto(n,\forall\varphi)$; so the equation holds by definition (reflexivity).

possible_uncertainties_v2: The default element returned when the first component is zero is irrelevant to the statement; the type of the default (it uses an Inhabited structure on the sigma type) is not shown in the context.

theorem pilot_p227 {c : Cardinal} {n : ℕ} [n.AtLeastTwo] :
  c.lift ≤ Cardinal.beth (OfNat.ofNat n) ↔ c ≤ Cardinal.beth (OfNat.ofNat n)
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $c$ be a cardinal number in some universe $u$, let $v$ be another universe and let $\mathrm{lift}(c)$ be its lift to the universe $\max(u,v)$. Let $n\ge2$ be a natural number (a numeral, viewed as an ordinal) and $\beth_n$ the $n$-th beth number, where $\beth_0=\aleph_0$, $\beth_{o+1}=2^{\beth_o}$ and $\beth_o=\sup_{a<o}\beth_a$ for limit ordinals $o$. Then $\mathrm{lift}(c)\le\beth_n$ (with $\beth_n$ computed in the universe $\max(u,v)$) if and only if $c\le\beth_n$ (with $\beth_n$ computed in universe $u$).
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $c$ be a cardinal number and let $n\ge 2$ be a natural number (written as a numeral). Let $\beth_n$ denote the $n$-th beth number. Then the universe-lift of $c$ is at most $\beth_n$ (computed in the larger universe) if and only if $c\le \beth_n$ (computed in the original universe).
proof_strategy: This is the special case of the same statement for an arbitrary natural number $n$: apply the order-preserving property of lift together with the fact that lifting commutes with $\beth_n$.
faithful_informal_proof: The numeral $n$ viewed as an ordinal is the cast of the natural number $n$, so the statement is literally the statement for natural number $n$. That one follows from the fact that lift is an order embedding, $\mathrm{lift}(c)\le\mathrm{lift}(d)\iff c\le d$, applied to $d=\beth_n$ together with $\mathrm{lift}(\beth_n)=\beth_n$ (lift commutes with the beth function and fixes finite ordinals).

lift of a beth number is the beth number of the lifted ordinal
lift of a natural-number ordinal is itself
numeral equals natural-number cast

theorem_in_words_v2: Let $k$ be a ring, $V$ an abelian group that is a $k$-module, and $P$ an affine space over $V$ (a set on which $V$ acts freely and transitively by translations, i.e. an additive torsor). Let $s_1,s_2$ be affine subspaces of $P$ over $k$ (subsets that are either empty or of the form $q+W$ for a point $q$ and a $k$-submodule $W\subseteq V$), and suppose a point $p\in P$ lies in both $s_1$ and $s_2$. The direction of an affine subspace $s$ is the $k$-submodule of $V$ consisting of the difference vectors $p_1-p_2$ with $p_1,p_2\in s$. Let $s_1\sqcup s_2$ be the join of $s_1$ and $s_2$ (the smallest affine subspace containing both, namely the affine span of $s_1\cup s_2$). Then the direction of $s_1\sqcup s_2$ equals the sum (join) of submodules $\mathrm{dir}(s_1)+\mathrm{dir}(s_2)$ of $V$.

Let $s_1,s_2$ be affine subspaces of $P$ and suppose a point $p$ lies in both $s_1$ and $s_2$. Then the direction (the underlying linear subspace of $V$) of the join $s_1\sqcup s_2$ (the smallest affine subspace containing both) equals the sum of the directions of $s_1$ and $s_2$.

Apply this with $p_1=p_2=p$: then $p_2-p_1=0$, the span $k\cdot0$ is the zero submodule, and adding it changes nothing, leaving $\mathrm{dir}(s_1)+\mathrm{dir}(s_2)$.

theorem pilot_p229 {p : Polynomial ℤ} (hp : p ≠ 0) :
  1 ≤ (Polynomial.map (Int.castRingHom ℂ) p).mahlerMeasure
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $p\in\mathbb Z[X]$ be a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients, and let $\tilde p\in\mathbb C[X]$ be the polynomial obtained by mapping its coefficients into $\mathbb C$ through the canonical ring homomorphism $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$. Then the Mahler measure of $\tilde p$ is at least $1$: $1\le M(\tilde p)$. (Here $M(q)$ for a nonzero complex polynomial $q$ is the geometric mean of $|q|$ over the unit circle, $M(q)=\exp\int_0^1\log|q(e^{2\pi it})|\,dt$, which also equals $|\mathrm{lc}(q)|\prod_{q(z)=0}\max(1,|z|)$ over the roots counted with multiplicity.)
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $p$ be a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients. Then the Mahler measure of $p$, viewed as a polynomial with complex coefficients, is at least $1$.
proof_strategy: Compare with the modulus of the leading coefficient, which is a nonzero integer, hence of absolute value at least one.
faithful_informal_proof: The Mahler measure of a complex polynomial is at least the modulus of its leading coefficient, so it suffices to show $1\le|\mathrm{lc}(\tilde p)|$. The map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ is injective, so the leading coefficient of $\tilde p$ is the image of the leading coefficient $n$ of $p$. Since $p\ne0$, $n$ is a nonzero integer. The modulus of the image of $n$ in $\mathbb C$ equals the absolute value $|n|$ (cast compatibility), and a nonzero integer has absolute value at least $1$. Thus $1\le|n|\le M(\tilde p)$.
used_key_ideas: Mahler measure is bounded below by the modulus of the leading coefficient
The canonical map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ is injective, so leading coefficients are preserved
A nonzero integer has absolute value at least $1$
possible_uncertainties_v2: The definition of the Mahler measure is not given in the file context; the description given is the standard one and is only used through the lower bound by the leading coefficient.

theorem_in_words_v2: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, $\iota$ an index type and $(s_i)_{i\in\iota}$ a family of $R$-modules (each $s_i$ an additive commutative monoid with an $R$-action, a module over the semiring $R$). The tensor product $\bigotimes_{i,R}s_i$ is the quotient of the free additive monoid on the set $R\times\prod_{i}s_i$ (formal finite sums of pairs $(r,(m_i)_i)$) by the additive congruence generated by the multilinearity relations; write $\pi$ for the quotient map to $\bigotimes_{i,R}s_i$. For an element $x\in\bigotimes_{i,R}s_i$ a lift of $x$ is an element $p$ of the free additive monoid with $\pi(p)=x$ (equivalently, $x=\sum_{(a,m)\in p}a\cdot\bigotimes_im_i$, summed over the entries $(a,m)$ of $p$). Let $x,y\in\bigotimes_{i,R}s_i$ and let $p,q$ be elements of the free additive monoid on $R\times\prod_is_i$. If $p$ is a lift of $x$ and $q$ is a lift of $y$, then $p+q$ (concatenation of formal sums) is a lift of $x+y$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring and $(s_i)_{i\in\iota}$ a family of $R$-modules, and consider the tensor product $\bigotimes_{i} s_i$ over $R$. This tensor product is the quotient of the free additive monoid on pairs $(r,(m_i)_i)$ with $r\in R$ and $m_i\in s_i$ by an additive congruence; an element $p$ of the free additive monoid is said to lift an element $x$ of the tensor product if $p$ is mapped to $x$ by the quotient map. The statement: if $p$ lifts $x$ and $q$ lifts $y$, then $p+q$ (concatenation of formal sums) lifts $x+y$.

faithful_informal_proof: Unfold membership in the set of lifts: $p$ lifts $x$ means $\pi(p)=x$, and $q$ lifts $y$ means $\pi(q)=y$. The quotient map $\pi$ is additive, so $\pi(p+q)=\pi(p)+\pi(q)$. Rewriting with the two hypotheses gives $\pi(p+q)=x+y$, i.e. $p+q$ lifts $x+y$.

theorem_in_words_v2:
Let $\alpha$ be a type equipped with an addition $+$, a binary relation $\le$, a least element $\bot$ (so $\bot\le a$ for all $a$) and a subtraction $-$ (no further axioms are assumed on $+$, $\le$ and $-$), such that $\alpha$ has ordered subtraction, i.e. $a-b\le c\iff a\le c+b$ for all $a,b,c\in\alpha$. Let $\alpha_\top=\alpha\cup\{\top\}$ be $\alpha$ with a top element adjoined (the elements are $\top$ and $\uparrow a$ for $a\in\alpha$), with the order $x\le y$ iff $y=\top$ or $x=\uparrow a$, $y=\uparrow b$ with $a\le b$; the addition $\top+x=x+\top=\top$ and $\uparrow a+\uparrow b=\uparrow(a+b)$; and the subtraction $\uparrow a-\uparrow b=\uparrow(a-b)$, $\top-\uparrow b=\top$, and $x-\top=\uparrow\bot$ for every $x$. Then $\alpha_\top$ also has ordered subtraction: for all $x,y,z\in\alpha_\top$,
$$x-y\le z\iff x\le z+y.$$
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $\alpha$ be a type with an addition, a partial order $\le$, a least element, and a subtraction, such that $\alpha$ satisfies the ordered-subtraction property: $a-b\le c\iff a\le b+c$ for all $a,b,c$. Let $\mathrm{WithTop}\,\alpha$ denote $\alpha$ with a greatest element $\top$ adjoined, with the induced addition and subtraction. Then $\mathrm{WithTop}\,\alpha$ also satisfies the ordered-subtraction property: $x-y\le z\iff x\le y+z$ for all $x,y,z\in\mathrm{WithTop}\,\alpha$.
proof_strategy: Case on whether $y$, $x$, $z$ are $\top$ or finite; the cases involving $\top$ are checked directly from the definitions, and the all-finite case reduces to ordered subtraction in $\alpha$.
faithful_informal_proof: Case on $y$. If $y=\top$, then $x-y=\uparrow\bot$ and $z+y=\top$; so the right side $x\le\top$ always holds, and the left side $\uparrow\bot\le z$ holds for every $z$ (for $z=\top$ trivially, for $z=\uparrow c$ since $\bot\le c$). Now let $y=\uparrow b$. If $x=\top$, then $x-y=\top$, and $\top\le z$ iff $z=\top$; on the other side $\top\le z+\uparrow b$ iff $z+\uparrow b=\top$ iff $z=\top$; so both sides agree. If $x=\uparrow a$ and $z=\top$, both sides hold ($x-y\le\top$ and $x\le\top+y=\top$). If $x=\uparrow a$, $z=\uparrow c$, then the statement becomes $\uparrow(a-b)\le\uparrow c\iff\uparrow a\le\uparrow(c+b)$, i.e. $a-b\le c\iff a\le c+b$, which is ordered subtraction in $\alpha$.

x - top = bottom and top - finite = top in the lifted subtraction
reduction of the finite case to ordered subtraction in the base

The orientation a - b <= c iff a <= c + b is taken from the final step of the proof (ordered subtraction in its right-hand form).

theorem pilot_p233 (X : AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme) {U : X.Opens}
  (f g : ↑(X.presheaf.obj (Opposite.op U))) : X.basicOpen (f + g) ≤ X.basicOpen f ⊔ X.basicOpen g
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $X$ be a scheme, $U\subseteq X$ an open subset, and let $f,g\in\Gamma(X,U)=\mathcal O_X(U)$ be two sections of the structure sheaf over $U$ (elements of the commutative ring $\mathcal O_X(U)$). For a section $s\in\mathcal O_X(U)$, let $X_s=\mathrm{basicOpen}(s)$ denote the open subset of $X$ consisting of the points $x\in U$ at which the germ $s_x$ of $s$ in the stalk $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a unit (the locus in $U$ where $s$ does not vanish). Then $$X_{f+g}\ \subseteq\ X_f\cup X_g,$$ that is, in the lattice of open subsets of $X$, $X_{f+g}\le X_f\sqcup X_g$ where $\sqcup$ is the union of open sets.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $X$ be a scheme, $U$ an open subset of $X$, and $f,g$ sections of the structure sheaf over $U$. Then the basic open set of $f+g$ is contained in the union of the basic open sets of $f$ and of $g$. (The basic open set of a section $s$ over $U$ is the set of points of $U$ at which the germ of $s$ is a unit in the stalk.)
proof_strategy: Take a point where $f+g$ has unit germ; since the stalk is a local ring and the germ of $f+g$ is the sum of the germs, one of the germs of $f,g$ is a unit.
faithful_informal_proof: Let $x\in X_{f+g}$. Then $x\in U$, since a basic open set is contained in $U$. Membership in the union is membership in one of the two sets, and for $x\in U$, $x\in X_s$ iff the germ of $s$ at $x$ is a unit in $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. The germ map $\mathcal O_X(U)\to\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a ring homomorphism, so the germ of $f+g$ at $x$ equals $f_x+g_x$, and by hypothesis it is a unit. The stalk $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a local ring (as $X$ is a scheme), and in a local ring if a sum of two elements is a unit then at least one of the two elements is a unit. Hence $f_x$ or $g_x$ is a unit, i.e. $x\in X_f$ or $x\in X_g$.

Germ map is a ring homomorphism
In a local ring, if $a+b$ is a unit then $a$ or $b$ is a unit

theorem_in_words_v2: Let $a,b,c$ be ordinals (in a fixed universe) and suppose $c$ is a limit ordinal in the sense of being a successor limit: $c\ne0$ and $c$ is not the successor of any ordinal. Then $a<b+c$ if and only if there exists an ordinal $d<c$ with $a<b+d$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $a,b,c$ be ordinals and suppose $c$ is a limit ordinal in the sense that it is nonzero and not a successor. Then $a<b+c$ if and only if there exists an ordinal $d<c$ with $a<b+d$.

theorem pilot_p235 {F : Type u} [Field F] {W : WeierstrassCurve.Jacobian F}
  {P : Fin 3 → F} (hPz : P 2 ≠ 0) :
  (MvPolynomial.eval P) W.polynomialX / P 2 ^ 4 =
    Polynomial.evalEval (P 0 / P 2 ^ 2) (P 1 / P 2 ^ 3) W.toAffine.polynomialX
theorem_in_words_v2:
Let $F$ be a field and let $W$ be a Weierstrass curve over $F$ with coefficients $a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,a_6$, in Jacobian coordinates. Its defining polynomial in three variables is $W(X,Y,Z)=Y^2+a_1XYZ+a_3YZ^3-(X^3+a_2X^2Z^2+a_4XZ^4+a_6Z^6)\in F[X,Y,Z]$, and $W_X=\partial W/\partial X=a_1YZ-(3X^2+2a_2XZ^2+a_4Z^4)$ is its partial derivative with respect to $X$. The affine Weierstrass polynomial of $W$ is $w(x,y)=y^2+a_1xy+a_3y-(x^3+a_2x^2+a_4x+a_6)\in F[x][y]$, with partial derivative with respect to $x$ equal to $w_x(x,y)=a_1y-(3x^2+2a_2x+a_4)$. For a triple $P=(P_0,P_1,P_2)\in F^3$ with $P_2\neq0$, the theorem states
$$\frac{W_X(P_0,P_1,P_2)}{P_2^{4}}=w_x\!\left(\frac{P_0}{P_2^{2}},\frac{P_1}{P_2^{3}}\right),$$
i.e. evaluating $W_X$ at $P$ and dividing by $P_2^4$ equals evaluating $w_x$ at the affine point $(P_0/P_2^2,\,P_1/P_2^3)$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $F$ be a field, $W$ a Weierstrass curve over $F$ in Jacobian coordinates, and $P=(P_0,P_1,P_2)\in F^3$ with $P_2\neq0$. Let $\partial_X$ denote the partial derivative with respect to $X$ of the Jacobian-coordinate defining polynomial of $W$ (a polynomial in three variables). Then evaluating this polynomial at $P$ and dividing by $P_2^4$ gives the same value as evaluating the partial derivative with respect to $X$ of the affine Weierstrass polynomial (in two variables) at the point $(P_0/P_2^2,\ P_1/P_2^3)$.
proof_strategy: Substitute the explicit formulas for both partial derivatives and verify the resulting identity of rational expressions in the coefficients and $P_0,P_1,P_2$ using $P_2\neq0$.
faithful_informal_proof: Evaluating the explicit expression for $W_X$ at $P$ gives $a_1P_1P_2-(3P_0^2+2a_2P_0P_2^2+a_4P_2^4)$, and evaluating the affine derivative at $(P_0/P_2^2,P_1/P_2^3)$ gives $a_1P_1/P_2^3-(3P_0^2/P_2^4+2a_2P_0/P_2^2+a_4)$. After dividing the first by $P_2^4$, the two sides agree term by term: $a_1P_1P_2/P_2^4=a_1P_1/P_2^3$, $3P_0^2/P_2^4$, $2a_2P_0P_2^2/P_2^4=2a_2P_0/P_2^2$, and $a_4P_2^4/P_2^4=a_4$. The needed cancellations $P_2/P_2=1$, $P_2^2/P_2^2=1$, $P_2^4/P_2^4=1$ all use $P_2\neq0$; formally, the identity is closed by a linear combination of the facts $P_2/P_2=1$, $P_2^2/P_2^2=1$, $P_2^4/P_2^4=1$ with the stated coefficients, after which the remaining equation is a polynomial-ring identity.

explicit formula for the affine partial derivative
cancellation of powers of P_2 using P_2 nonzero

lean_statement: theorem pilot_p236 {b : ℕ} (l : List ℕ) : Nat.ofDigits b (l ++ [0]) = Nat.ofDigits b l
theorem_in_words_v2: For a natural number $b$ (the base) and a list $L=[d_0,d_1,\dots,d_{k-1}]$ of natural numbers (little-endian digits), define $\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(L)=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}d_i b^i\in\mathbb N$; recursively, $\operatorname{ofDigits}_b([\,])=0$ and $\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(h::t)=h+b\cdot\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(t)$. The statement: for every base $b\in\mathbb N$ and every list $L$ of natural numbers, appending a trailing digit $0$ does not change the value, $\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(L\mathbin{+\!\!+}[0])=\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(L)$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $b$ be a natural number (the base) and $l$ a list of natural numbers (digits, least significant first). Then the number represented by the digit list $l$ followed by an extra digit $0$ in base $b$ equals the number represented by $l$.
proof_strategy: Use the formula for the value of a concatenation of two digit lists and compute the contribution of the one-element list $[0]$.
faithful_informal_proof: For concatenation one has $\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(L_1\mathbin{+\!\!+}L_2)=\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(L_1)+b^{|L_1|}\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(L_2)$. With $L_1=L$ and $L_2=[0]$, and since $\operatorname{ofDigits}_b([n])=n$, we get $\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(L\mathbin{+\!\!+}[0])=\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(L)+b^{|L|}\cdot0$. Now $b^{|L|}\cdot 0=0$ and adding $0$ changes nothing, giving $\operatorname{ofDigits}_b(L)$.
used_key_ideas: Value of a concatenation of digit lists
Value of a single-digit list
Multiplication by zero and adding zero

theorem pilot_p237
  (P : CategoryTheory.MorphismProperty AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme) [AlgebraicGeometry.IsZariskiLocalAtTarget P] :
  AlgebraicGeometry.HasAffineProperty P (AlgebraicGeometry.AffineTargetMorphismProperty.of P)
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $P$ be a property of morphisms of schemes (in a fixed universe) which is local at the target for the Zariski topology: it respects isomorphisms, is stable under restriction to open subschemes of the target (if $P$ holds for $f\colon X\to Y$ then it holds for $f|_U\colon f^{-1}(U)\to U$ for every open $U\subseteq Y$), and holds for $f$ as soon as it holds for the restrictions of $f$ to the members of some open cover of $Y$. Let $\mathrm{of}(P)$ be the affine target morphism property obtained by restricting $P$ to morphisms with affine target, i.e. the property which holds for $f\colon X\to Y$ with $Y$ affine exactly when $P$ holds for $f$. Then $(P,\mathrm{of}(P))$ has the affine-property structure, meaning: (1) $\mathrm{of}(P)$ is a local affine target property (it respects isomorphisms; if it holds for $f\colon X\to Y$ with $Y$ affine, it holds for the restriction of $f$ to $\mathrm{Spec}\,\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)_r=D(r)\subseteq Y$ for every global section $r$; and if it holds for the restrictions to the basic opens $D(r)$ for $r$ in a set of global sections generating the unit ideal, it holds for $f$); and (2) $P$ equals the property "for every affine open $U$ of the target $Y$ of $f$, $\mathrm{of}(P)$ holds for the restriction $f^{-1}(U)\to U$", i.e. $P(f)\iff \forall U\subseteq Y\text{ affine open},\ P(f|_U)$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $P$ be a property of morphisms of schemes that is local at the target for the Zariski topology (it can be checked on an open cover of the target, and is stable under restriction to opens of the target). Then $P$ has the affine-property structure given by the affine target property `of P`, namely the restriction of $P$ to morphisms whose target is affine: this affine property is local on affine targets, and $P$ is equal to the property of morphisms $f:X\to Y$ such that for every affine open $U\subseteq Y$ the restriction $f^{-1}(U)\to U$ satisfies the affine property.
proof_strategy: Condition (1) follows from the standing assumption that $P$ is Zariski local at the target, via a known instance; for (2), the forward implication is stability under restriction, and the backward one uses the affine open cover of $Y$ together with locality of $P$ at the target.
faithful_informal_proof: Condition (1), that the affine target property $\mathrm{of}(P)$ is local, is supplied directly by the known fact (an instance) that the restriction of a Zariski-local-at-target property to affine targets is a local affine target property. For condition (2), the equality of properties, take schemes $X,Y$ and $f\colon X\to Y$ and prove both implications. ($\Rightarrow$) If $P(f)$ holds, then for every affine open $U\subseteq Y$, $P(f|_U)$ holds by stability of $P$ under restriction to opens of the target, i.e. $\mathrm{of}(P)$ holds for $f|_U$. ($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $P(f|_U)$ holds for all affine opens $U$ of $Y$. Cover $Y$ by its standard affine open cover $\{U_i\}$; to show $P(f)$ it suffices, by locality of $P$ at the target, to show that $P$ holds for the base change of $f$ along each inclusion $U_i\to Y$. Each such base change is a pullback square exhibiting $f^{-1}(U_i)\to U_i$ as the pullback of $f$ along the open immersion, and the hypothesis on the affine open $U_i$ gives $P$ for it by the lemma that if a property holds affine-locally and a square is a pullback then the corresponding base change satisfies it.

P holds for f iff it holds over every member of an open cover of the target
the standard affine open cover of a scheme
restriction of f to an open of the target is a pullback along the open immersion
ext: equality of morphism properties proved by both implications

The definition of the restriction of P to affine targets is inferred from its docstring, and the form of the lemma on pullback squares used for the reverse implication is inferred.
The three conditions defining a local affine property are taken from the docstring of the corresponding class.

theorem_in_words_v2:
Let $(\alpha,\mathcal{M})$ be a measurable space and $\mu$ a probability measure on it. Let $f:\alpha\to\mathbb{R}$ be $\mu$-integrable, and let $N\subseteq\alpha$ be a set (not necessarily measurable) with $\mu(N)=0$ (outer measure zero). Then there exists a point $x\in\alpha$ with $x\notin N$ and
$$\int_\alpha f\,d\mu\;\le\;f(x).$$
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on a measurable space $\alpha$, let $f:\alpha\to\mathbb{R}$ be $\mu$-integrable, and let $N$ be a set with $\mu(N)=0$. Then there exists a point $x\notin N$ with $\int f\,d\mu\le f(x)$.
proof_strategy: For a probability measure the average equals the integral, so this is the first-moment-method statement for the average, applied with the nonzero measure $\mu$.
faithful_informal_proof: Since $\mu$ is a probability measure, the average $\frac{1}{\mu(\alpha)}\int f\,d\mu$ equals $\int f\,d\mu$, and $\mu\ne0$. The analogous result for averages (for a nonzero finite measure, an integrable real function $f$, and a null set $N$, there is $x\notin N$ with $\fint f\,d\mu\le f(x)$) therefore applies, and rewriting the average as the integral gives the claim.
used_key_ideas: For a probability measure, average equals integral
First moment method for the average, avoiding a null set
possible_uncertainties_v2: The average version (exists_notMem_null_average_le) is cited as a black box; its own proof (that the set where f is at least the average has positive measure, hence is not contained in a null set) is not shown.

theorem_in_words_v2: Let $\alpha$ and $\Omega$ be measurable spaces, let $\kappa$ be a kernel from $\alpha$ to $\Omega$, and let $\mu$ be a measure on $\alpha$. Let $\iota$ be an index type and $(s_i)_{i\in\iota}$ a family of subsets of $\Omega$ (no measurability assumed). Let $\beta$ be a type with distinguished elements $0$ and $1$ (not assumed distinct) and with a measurable space structure. Say that the family of sets $(s_i)$ is independent with respect to $\kappa$ and $\mu$ if the family of $\sigma$-algebras $\sigma(\{s_i\})=\{\emptyset,s_i,s_i^c,\Omega\}$ is independent, i.e. for every finite $S\subseteq\iota$ and every choice of sets $t_i\in\sigma(\{s_i\})$, $i\in S$, we have, for $\mu$-almost every $a\in\alpha$, $\kappa(a)(\bigcap_{i\in S}t_i)=\prod_{i\in S}\kappa(a)(t_i)$. Say that a family of functions $(f_i)_{i\in\iota}$, $f_i\colon\Omega\to\beta$, is independent with respect to $\kappa$ and $\mu$ if the family of $\sigma$-algebras $f_i^{-1}(\mathcal B_\beta)=\{f_i^{-1}(B): B\text{ measurable in }\beta\}$ is independent in the same sense: for every finite $S$ and every choice of measurable $B_i\subseteq\beta$ ($i\in S$), for $\mu$-a.e. $a$, $\kappa(a)(\bigcap_{i\in S}f_i^{-1}(B_i))=\prod_{i\in S}\kappa(a)(f_i^{-1}(B_i))$. Statement: if $(s_i)_{i\in\iota}$ is independent with respect to $\kappa$ and $\mu$, then the family of indicator functions $f_i=\mathbf 1_{s_i}\colon\Omega\to\beta$ (value $1$ on $s_i$ and $0$ off $s_i$) is independent with respect to $\kappa$ and $\mu$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $\kappa$ be a kernel from $\alpha$ to $\Omega$ and $\mu$ a measure on $\alpha$. Let $(s_i)_{i\in\iota}$ be a family of subsets of $\Omega$ that is mutually independent with respect to $\kappa$ and $\mu$ (as sets, via the $\sigma$-algebras they generate). Let $\beta$ be a type with elements $0$ and $1$ and a $\sigma$-algebra. Then the family of indicator functions $\omega\mapsto \mathbf{1}_{s_i}(\omega)$ (taking value $1$ on $s_i$ and $0$ elsewhere) is mutually independent as random variables with respect to $\kappa$ and $\mu$.
proof_strategy: Use the product-formula characterisation of independence of functions; the preimage of any set under an indicator is a union of $s_i$, its complement, or empty pieces, hence lies in the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $s_i$, so the set independence hypothesis applies.
faithful_informal_proof: Independence of a family of functions is equivalent to the statement that for every finite index set $S$ and measurable sets $B_i\subseteq\beta$, $\mu$-almost surely $\kappa(a)(\bigcap_{i\in S}f_i^{-1}(B_i))=\prod_{i\in S}\kappa(a)(f_i^{-1}(B_i))$. Fix $S$ and the $B_i$. For the indicator $f_i=\mathbf 1_{s_i}$ with values $1$ and $0$, the preimage of $B_i$ is $f_i^{-1}(B_i)=(\text{if }1\in B_i\text{ then }s_i\text{ else }\emptyset)\ \cup\ (\text{if }0\in B_i\text{ then }s_i^c\text{ else }\emptyset)$. Each of the two pieces belongs to the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $s_i$ (namely $s_i$, $s_i^c$, or $\emptyset$), and hence so does the union. The independence of the family $(s_i)$, which says the product formula holds for arbitrary sets in the generated $\sigma$-algebras, therefore yields the desired product formula for the sets $f_i^{-1}(B_i)$.
used_key_ideas: characterisation of independence of functions by the product formula on preimages
preimage of a set under a constant-valued indicator is a union of s, s^c or empty pieces
these sets lie in the sigma-algebra generated by s

lean_statement: theorem pilot_p241 {c : Cardinal} : Cardinal.aleph 1 < c.lift ↔ Cardinal.aleph 1 < c
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $c$ be a cardinal number in some universe $u$, let $v$ be another universe, and $\mathrm{lift}(c)$ its lift to universe $\max(u,v)$. Let $\aleph_1$ denote the first uncountable cardinal, i.e. the successor of $\aleph_0$ (the second infinite cardinal $\aleph_{1}$ in the aleph enumeration $\aleph_0,\aleph_1,\dots$ of infinite cardinals). Then $\aleph_1<\mathrm{lift}(c)$ (with $\aleph_1$ in universe $\max(u,v)$) if and only if $\aleph_1<c$ (with $\aleph_1$ in universe $u$).
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $c$ be a cardinal number. Then $\aleph_1<\mathrm{lift}(c)$ if and only if $\aleph_1<c$, where $\mathrm{lift}$ denotes the lift of a cardinal to a higher universe and $\aleph_1$ is the first uncountable cardinal (in the corresponding universe).
proof_strategy: Lift is a strictly monotone embedding and fixes $\aleph_1$, so $\aleph_1<c$ iff $\mathrm{lift}(\aleph_1)<\mathrm{lift}(c)$ iff $\aleph_1<\mathrm{lift}(c)$.
faithful_informal_proof: Since lift is an order embedding, $\mathrm{lift}(a)<\mathrm{lift}(c)\iff a<c$; apply this with $a=\aleph_1$. By the simplification lemmas, $\mathrm{lift}(\aleph_1)=\aleph_1$ (lift commutes with the aleph function and lift of the ordinal $1$ is $1$), so the left-hand side becomes $\aleph_1<\mathrm{lift}(c)$, which gives the stated equivalence.
used_key_ideas: lift preserves and reflects strict order on cardinals
lift of aleph is aleph of the lifted ordinal
lift of the ordinal 1 is 1
possible_uncertainties_v2: That the simp step uses the commutation of lift with the aleph function is inferred from standard simp lemmas rather than shown in the file context.

theorem pilot_p242 {n : ℕ} {c : ℂ} :
  Polynomial.toAddCircle ((Polynomial.monomial n) c) = c • fourier ↑n
theorem_in_words_v2: Let $n$ be a natural number and $c\in\mathbb{C}$. Let $T=2\pi$ and let $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ be the additive circle of period $2\pi$. The map $\Phi:\mathbb{C}[X]\to C(\mathbb{T},\mathbb{C})$ is the $\mathbb{C}$-algebra homomorphism that evaluates a polynomial on the unit circle: $\Phi(p)(\theta)=p(e^{i\theta})$ for $\theta\in\mathbb{T}$ (it is the algebra map determined by sending $X$ to the continuous function $\theta\mapsto e^{i\theta}$). For $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ let $e_m(\theta)=e^{im\theta}$ be the $m$-th Fourier character on $\mathbb{T}$. Then for the monomial $cX^n$ one has $\Phi(cX^n)=c\cdot e_n$ as continuous functions on $\mathbb{T}$, where $n$ is viewed as an integer and $c\cdot e_n$ is the scalar multiple of $e_n$ by $c$.
theorem_in_words_v1: Let $n$ be a natural number and $c$ a complex number. Consider the map sending a polynomial with complex coefficients to the function it defines on the circle, i.e. on the additive circle, by evaluating the polynomial at the point of the unit circle corresponding to $\theta$. Then the image of the monomial $c X^n$ is $c$ times the $n$-th Fourier character $\theta\mapsto e_n(\theta)$ (the character of the additive circle with integer index $n$).
proof_strategy: Check equality of continuous functions pointwise: evaluating the monomial at $e^{i\theta}$ gives $c\,e^{in\theta}$, and the $n$th power of the circle point is the circle point of $n\theta$.
faithful_informal_proof: Equality of continuous functions is checked at each $\theta\in\mathbb{T}$. By definition of $\Phi$ as polynomial evaluation at the circle point $z=e^{i\theta}$, the value of $\Phi(cX^n)$ at $\theta$ is $c\,z^n=c\,(e^{i\theta})^n$. The $n$th power of the circle point of $\theta$ equals the circle point of $n\theta$ (the circle point map is a homomorphism, so $e^{i n\theta}=(e^{i\theta})^n$), which is $e_n(\theta)$. So the value at $\theta$ is $c\,e_n(\theta)$, which is the value of $c\cdot e_n$.
used_key_ideas: algebra map is polynomial evaluation at the unit-circle point
power of the circle point equals circle point of the multiple (character property)
possible_uncertainties_v2: The circle point of $\theta$ is exp(i*theta) as the period is $2\pi$; this follows from the docstring of the evaluation map but the identification of the Fourier character with exp(i n theta) uses the standard definition, which is not in the file context.
